cards.text: This is 1 Chronicles, and it opens with one big family tree, starting at the very top with Adam, the first man (1 Corinthians 15:45). No ages, no stories, just names, like the book walked in and started reading the guest list. The names run down to the man who went into the ark because of the flood (Genesis 7:7).

cards.question: The list runs from Adam down to the man who went into the ark. Who is he?
Then the family tree splits three ways. Noah's sons are Shem, Ham and ___.

cards.text: Next come the families that came from Noah's three sons. Two names stand out. Nimrod began to be a mighty one on the earth. And Peleg got his name because in his days the earth was divided. Imagine your whole lifetime getting summed up by one headline.
Then the list zooms in on one line from Shem: Arphaxad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg, and on down through Terah. Friend, I spent years counting dust in a junk drawer, and even I'm ready for a familiar face.

cards.question: After all those names, the line from Shem finally lands on a name you KNOW. Who is it?
True or false: Abraham's sons are Isaac and Esau.

cards.text: Ishmael has twelve sons, starting with his firstborn, Nebaioth. Then Keturah, Abraham's concubine, has six more sons, and Midian is one of them. That family reunion needs a BIGGER yard.

cards.question: Abraham's son Isaac has two sons. Who are they?

cards.text: Israel is the man also called Jacob (Genesis 32:28). The list follows Esau's family, Amalek among them, and then the family of Seir the Horite (Genesis 36:20). That's a LOT of cousins, friend. You'd need a whole group chat just to plan the cookie exchange.

cards.question: The list turns to the kings of Edom. True or false: they reigned before any king reigned over the Israelites.

cards.text: Eight kings reign in Edom. Over and over, a king dies and someone reigns in his place, until the last one, Hadad, dies. Then comes a list of Edom's chiefs, and that's the whole chapter, friend. You just walked from Adam all the way to Edom without breaking a sweat.

findings.problem: The whole passage is a genealogy and name list, with the list of Edom's kings at the end. The docs say a long stretch is summed up in one story card, never gets a choice card, and the baker should not have to memorize it. They also say a stretch never gets a stop of its own and that its card sits with the moments around it. Here there are no moments around it. The walkthrough splits the genealogy into five summary story cards (4, 5, 8, 10, 12). It also asks six choice cards about details inside the lists: card 2 (Noah), card 3 (Japheth), card 6 (Abraham), card 7 (Abraham's sons), card 9 (Isaac's sons) and card 11 (the kings of Edom came before Israel's kings). Card 3 in particular asks the baker to recall a name from the list.
findings.question: When an entire passage is a long stretch, like 1 Chronicles 1, how should Prep handle it? Can it break the stretch into several summary cards? Can it ask choice cards about the key names or turning points, like Noah, Abraham, Isaac's sons, or the note that Edom had kings before Israel? Or should it be a single summary card, with the usual rule that choice cards equal or outnumber story cards set aside?

findings.problem: Cards 4, 10 and 12 have four sentences each, and card 8 has three. The bite-sized rule allows 1 to 2 sentences on every story card except the opening card. However, the doc's own good example of a summary card for a long stretch (Genesis 5) has four sentences.
findings.question: Can a summary story card for a long stretch go past the 1 to 2 sentence limit, as the Genesis 5 example does? If so, how long can it be?

findings.problem: Card 8 opens with "Ishmael has twelve sons" and never says who Ishmael is. Ishmael was only the hidden right answer behind card 7's false statement. A baker who correctly marked card 7 False never sees Ishmael's name before this card, so they have no idea he is Abraham's son.

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: Most choice cards can only be answered from outside knowledge or by luck. Card 3 (Japheth), card 7 (Isaac and Ishmael, with no story card before it), card 9 (Esau and Israel, with no story card before it) and card 11 (Edom's kings reigning before Israel's) are all discovery questions. Only cards 2 and 6 are set up so the baker can reason toward the answer.

rule.text: A few discovery questions are fine. Some moments can't be reasoned out, like where Jonah's ship is headed. A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

findings.problem: The joke "I spent years counting dust in a junk drawer, and even I'm ready for a familiar face" gets its laugh from the Scripture list being so tedious that even someone who counted dust is worn out by it. The target is the passage itself, not Papa Dorin.

rule.text: His humor never targets God, Jesus, Scripture or the Marriage Supper.

findings.problem: The humor across the walkthrough is mild and pleasant rather than laugh-out-loud. Examples are "You just walked from Adam all the way to Edom without breaking a sweat" (card 12) and "That family reunion needs a BIGGER yard" (card 8). These read like a nice dad being pleasant.

rule.text: If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
